title: Find the CO₂ in the air
hook: You breathe out carbon dioxide all day. How much of the air around you is it?

knows: that air is a mixture of gases
that a drop holds about 10^21 molecules (molecules-in-one-drop)
doesNotKnow: what a share of a few parts per million looks like
that a tiny share can still be an enormous count

misconception: Carbon dioxide is a sizeable part of air (several per cent or more), and 'a few parts per million' means 'almost none there'.
objective: The learner can say that only about 4 in 10,000 molecules of dry air are CO2 (about 420 ppm, 0.042%), and that this tiny share is still about 5 x 10^18 molecules in one breath.

claims.text: Dry air is about 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen and 0.93% argon by volume (molecule count): of 10,000 molecules, 7,808 nitrogen, 2,095 oxygen and 93 argon (stage legend; reveal: 'Of your 10,000 dots, 7,808 were nitrogen, 2,095 oxygen, 93 argon').
claims.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 'Composition of dry air' / U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 (N2 78.084%, O2 20.946%, Ar 0.934%). Per 10,000: 7,808.4, 2,094.6, 93.4, rounded. Brief claim 1.

claims.text: Carbon dioxide is about 420 parts per million of the atmosphere, 0.042%, about 4 of every 10,000 molecules (question answer; stage legend 'CO₂ 4'; reveal: 'only 4 carbon dioxide: about 420 parts per million, or 0.042%').
claims.source: WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin No. 20 (October 2024): global mean 420.0 ppm for 2023; cross-check NOAA GML or Scripps Mauna Loa records. 420 ppm = 4.2 per 10,000 = 0.042%. Brief claim 2.

claims.text: The grid's 7,808 + 2,095 + 93 + 4 = 10,000 rounds each share and leaves out gases under 1 per 10,000 (neon, helium, methane, krypton, hydrogen and others, about 27 ppm in total).
claims.source: Node arithmetic (demo-builder 2026-10-14) from c1 and c2. Not stated to the learner; disclosed here. Brief claim 3.

claims.text: One breath of about 0.5 L of air at 25 °C and 1 atm holds about 5 x 10^18 CO2 molecules (stage: 'One breath, about 0.5 L: about 5 × 10¹⁸ CO₂ molecules'; reveal).
claims.source: n = PV/RT = 101,325 Pa x 0.0005 m^3 / (8.314 x 298.15) = 0.0204 mol; x 6.02214076e23 x 420e-6 = 5.2e18 (node). Tidal volume about 0.5 L at rest: Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology, pulmonary ventilation. Brief claim 4.

claims.text: A part per million is a share, not an amount; a tiny share of a huge crowd is still a huge number, which is why trace gases are counted in ppm (reveal).
claims.source: Definition: 1 ppm = 1 part in 10^6 by count (mole fraction, for gases), e.g. IUPAC Gold Book on 'parts per million'; the 'huge number' follows from c4.

claims.text: The dot positions are a seeded layout, not a sample of real air (mulberry32, seed 42; seed picked so the four CO2 rings sit apart and away from the edge, which does not change any count).
claims.source: The lesson (Demo.tsx layout()). Brief claim 5; pattern disclose-chosen-seeds.

recall.question: A gas makes up 2 parts per million of the air. In one litre of air, is there a lot of it or almost none?
options: Almost none: 2 ppm rounds to zero
A lot: still about 5 x 10^16 molecules
recall.why: Parts per million is a share. A litre of air holds about 2.5 x 10^22 molecules, so 2 per million of them is still about 5 x 10^16 molecules.
